title: Palace, several senators reject proposed coffee tax
summary: Malacañang and several senators on Friday expressed opposition to a proposal to impose taxes on coffee products.
byline: GISELLE OMBAY, TINA PANGANIBAN-PEREZ, GMA News

blocks.text: Malacañang and several senators on Friday expressed opposition to a proposal to impose taxes on coffee products.
In a statement, Presidential Legislative Liaison Office Secretary Joey Salceda said the government opposes taxing coffee itself.

"If more Filipinos are drinking coffee instead of alcohol, that is a good thing. It means that sin taxes on alcohol are working as designed. Simply put, you can drive after drinking coffee. You should not drive after drinking alcohol. The distinction is that simple," Salceda said.

During the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P378.629-billion budget of the Department of Health (DOH) and its attached agencies and corporations for 2027, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also opposed the proposal, noting that coffee is widely consumed in the Philippines.
He said that even workers who render overtime rely on coffee to stay awake.

"Personally, I don't think taxing coffee is a good idea. Well, first of all, coffee drinker po ang Pilipinas. Ang dami ngang Starbucks dito, ang daming mga coffee shops. Naging pastime natin 'yan," he said.
(Personally, I don't think taxing coffee is a good idea. First of all, the Philippines has many coffee drinkers. There are so many Starbucks and coffee shops. Drinking coffee has become our pastime.)
"We should also be sensitive to the products that our farmers, fishermen, and also our ordinary kababayans drink if they want to go overtime," he added.
Gatchalian also welcomed the commitment of House members not to pursue any proposal to tax coffee products.
The proposal to tax coffee in the Philippines was earlier raised by Olivia Limpe-Aw, president of the Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines.
Senator Pia Cayetano, meanwhile, welcomed the statement of House ways and means committee chairperson Miro Quimbo that any proposal to impose taxes on coffee products was "dead for good."
"So hindi na 'yan makakarating sa 'tin kasi I'm one with you na 'yung product nga na 'yun, tinutulungan nga natin 'yung farmers," Cayetano said.
(So that will no longer reach the Senate because I share your view that the product actually helps our farmers.)
"On that note, buhay pa rin ang kape sa Pilipinas (the coffee industry in the Philippines is still alive). No tax, no tax on coffee!" she added.
Senator Joel Villanueva also weighed in on the proposal.
"'Pag 'yan ang pinag-usapan, Mr. President, maghahalo ang tinalupan sa binalatan (If that matter is discussed, Mr. President, all hell will break loose)," Villanueva said.
Tax on 3-in-1 coffee?
Meanwhile, Quimbo said 3-in-1 coffee could be subjected to taxation in the next few years if manufacturers fail to reduce the sugar content of their products.
Unlike regular coffee, 3-in-1 coffee contains sugar and other caloric ingredients, making it a potential candidate for inclusion in the sweetened beverage tax, he explained.
Quimbo said 3-in-1 coffee was exempted from the sweetened beverage tax when it was first implemented several years ago because it was widely consumed by ordinary Filipinos.
However, he noted that manufacturers have since increased the sugar content of their products.
Some members of the House of Representatives have proposed imposing a tax on 3-in-1 coffee, Quimbo said.
However, he said his committee was not inclined to support the proposal, citing the product's widespread consumption among lower-income Filipinos.
Still, Quimbo stressed the need to consider the health effects of excessive sugar consumption and encourage manufacturers to reduce the sugar content of their products.
He said manufacturers could be given a three-year transition period to reformulate their products and lower their sugar content.
Otherwise, 3-in-1 coffee products exceeding a measurable sugar threshold could be subjected to taxation after the transition period, he added.
Salceda said proposals to extend the sweetened beverage tax to sweetened coffee, including 3-in-1 mixes, should be evaluated on their own merits and not based on declining alcohol tax revenues.
"Sin taxes are punitive by design. They are meant to discourage socially undesirable behavior, not to compensate for declining revenues from other sin taxes," he said. —VBL, GMA News
